title: Absorbing Louis, Chick Webb's critique and ballads
summary: Roy imitated Louis but kept to his own style; Chick Webb said he was fast but saying nothing, so he returned to Coleman's ballads.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Sound(? ) good, man. You know, by that time I had really got indoctrinated with Louis to the point that I was going around trying to talk like him. You know, [POPS GROWL] "Yeah, urrgghh, yeah..." -- you know... And I went through that phase. But I never did get him so tight that I played exactly like him, you know.

You see, I think I was smart enough to know there were certain things I had to play to get through. Because I remember when my brother was trying to get me established around here, he had me in the Rhythm Club playing, you know, and I broke it up, but Chick Webb said, "He's fast but he ain't sayin' nothin'." That's the whole story, you dig. That's like I say, you get something, and you rehearse it and you rehearse it, and then you can play it fast and precisely. But what are you saying?

So I knew, like, that would have to happen, and I started to listen to Coleman again, you know, them ballads he was playing. I got back on that kick. Because I never did listen to Coleman... Coleman didn't play too much
ballads way back there, you know. Everything with me had to be skittin'.
Well, I guess the Henderson band didn't go in much for ballads until the early Thirties or so. It was mostly...the way Coleman used to say, it was a stomp band.
Although Joe Smith used to play some pretty things.
